question: This athlete lost a January 2022 court appeal and was deported before the year's first major, which he had won the previous three times it was held. This man completed a "double career Golden Slam" by winning gold in Paris in 2024, beating Carlos Alcaraz. In a 2021 final, Daniil Medvedev denied this man the first men's calendar-year Grand Slam since Rod Laver. (*) Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer each finished their careers with fewer major titles than this man, who has won a record ten Australian Opens. For 10 points, name this Serbian who holds the men's record of 24 Grand Slam singles titles.

Before drafting this player 199th overall, scouts panned his lackluster combine, which produced an infamously slow 40-yard dash and an unflattering shirtless photo. At Michigan, this player split time with Drew Henson. He led the largest comeback in Super Bowl history, erasing a (*) 28–3 deficit against the Falcons in overtime. After 20 seasons under Bill Belichick's franchise, he won his seventh ring with the Buccaneers. For 10 points, name this quarterback who won six Super Bowls with the New England Patriots.
answer: Tom Brady [or Thomas Edward Patrick Brady Jr.]

question: This team's fans once threw a stuffed billy goat onto the field, referencing a curse supposedly placed by tavern owner William Sianis. A fan of this team named Steve Bartman deflected a foul ball that Moisés Alou was attempting to catch in the 2003 NLCS. Broadcaster Harry Caray led renditions of "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" at this team's home park, which features (*) ivy-covered outfield walls. A rain-delay speech by Jason Heyward preceded this team's 10-inning Game 7 win over Cleveland. For 10 points, name this team that ended a 108-year World Series drought in 2016 at Wrigley Field.

This athlete's interpreter, Ippei Mizuhara, was sentenced to prison for stealing roughly seventeen million dollars from him to cover gambling debts. This player became the first member of the "50–50 club" with a six-hit, three-homer game in Miami in 2024. He won Rookie of the Year in 2018 with a team from Anaheim, then signed a (*) 700-million-dollar contract with heavy deferrals. Comparisons to Babe Ruth follow this man because he both pitches and hits. For 10 points, name this Japanese two-way superstar for the Los Angeles Dodgers.

This event's slowest winning time in decades came in 2019, when Country House won after Maximum Security was disqualified for interference. A 2021 winner of this race, Medina Spirit, was stripped of victory after failing a drug test, leading to a suspension for trainer Bob Baffert. Its winner receives a garland of (*) 554 red flowers, and attendees traditionally sip mint juleps. Dubbed "the most exciting two minutes in sports," it opens the Triple Crown each May at Churchill Downs. For 10 points, name this horse race held annually in Louisville.

During one edition of this event, an exhausted George Foreman was knocked out in the eighth round after his opponent leaned on the ropes for much of the fight, a tactic later dubbed "rope-a-dope." That edition of this bout was held in Zaire and promoted by Don King. The man who won it later fought Joe Frazier in the (*) "Thrilla in Manila." For 10 points, give the rhyming nickname of the 1974 heavyweight title fight in Kinshasa won by Muhammad Ali.
answer: the Rumble in the Jungle [accept descriptive answers about the Ali–Foreman fight before "Foreman"]

question: This player scored 13 points in the final 33 seconds of a 2004 game against San Antonio. After being drafted 13th overall by the Hornets, he was traded for Vlade Divac. This player airballed four late shots in a playoff loss to Utah as a rookie, but later won back-to-back titles alongside Pau Gasol. He scored (*) 60 points in his 2016 finale against the Jazz and 81 against the Raptors in 2006, the second-most in NBA history. For 10 points, name this five-time champion Lakers guard nicknamed the "Black Mamba," who died in a 2020 helicopter crash.

This athlete withdrew from the team final at one Olympics after experiencing the "twisties," then returned to take bronze on beam. Two skills named for this athlete on vault include the Yurchenko double pike, which she landed in international competition in 2023. At the 2024 Paris Games, she anchored the American "Redemption Tour" team and won three golds, including the (*) all-around. For 10 points, name this American often called the greatest gymnast of all time.
answer: Simone Biles [or Simone Arianne Biles Owens]

question: This trophy was once drop-kicked into Ottawa's Rideau Canal, and a team once left it on the side of a road after changing a flat tire. Each member of a winning team traditionally spends a day with this trophy, which is accompanied at all times by a white-gloved "keeper." Misspellings engraved on it include (*) "BQSTQN" for Boston. Rings are added to and removed from its barrel-shaped body as it fills with names. For 10 points, name this oldest North American professional sports trophy, awarded to the NHL champion.

This player's junior-year team lost the national title game to Kim Mulkey's LSU squad, during which Angel Reese taunted her with a "you can't see me" gesture. In 2024, this player broke Pete Maravich's all-time NCAA Division I scoring record. Known for logo-range three-pointers at (*) Iowa, she was selected first overall in the 2024 WNBA draft and won Rookie of the Year. For 10 points, name this guard for the Indiana Fever widely credited with exploding women's basketball viewership.

This man scored a bicycle kick against Juventus in a Champions League quarterfinal that earned a standing ovation from the opposing fans, who signed him a year later. This player won the Euro in 2016 with his national team and left Real Madrid as its all-time leading scorer. After a second stint at (*) Manchester United ended with a explosive Piers Morgan interview, he joined Al-Nassr of the Saudi Pro League. For 10 points, name this Portuguese rival of Lionel Messi.

This coach went 9–2 in his lone NFL season-and-change with the Dolphins before abruptly leaving, telling reporters "I'm not going to be the Alabama coach" days before taking exactly that job. He won his first national title at LSU in 2003. His "Process" produced six national championships at his final school, where he lost his last game to (*) Michigan in the Rose Bowl before retiring in January 2024 and joining ESPN's College GameDay. For 10 points, name this coach of the Crimson Tide dynasty.
answer: Nick Saban [or Nicholas Lou Saban Jr.]

question: A contested finish to one season in this sport occurred when race director Michael Masi allowed only some lapped cars to un-lap themselves in Abu Dhabi, setting up a final-lap pass on fresher tires. Netflix's Drive to Survive dramatically boosted this sport's American popularity, leading to new races in Miami and (*) Las Vegas. Max Verstappen won four straight championships in this sport, whose record for career wins is held by a driver who moved to Ferrari in 2025. For 10 points, name this open-wheel racing series contested by Lewis Hamilton.

In this game's most famous play, David Tyree made a "helmet catch" by pinning the ball against his head while being dragged down by Rodney Harrison. Eli Manning escaped a near-sack to throw that pass. The losing team in this game entered (*) 18–0, seeking the first perfect season since the 1972 Dolphins. For 10 points, name this February 2008 championship game in which the Giants stunned the previously undefeated Patriots.
answer: Super Bowl XLII [or Super Bowl 42; accept 2008 Super Bowl; prompt on "Super Bowl"]

question: This athlete's father took out a full-page thank-you ad in a Milwaukee newspaper after his son was traded. While with a Japanese team, this athlete set the single-season professional record later broken—actually never broken—of 262 hits, set in MLB in 2004. He won both MVP and Rookie of the Year in (*) 2001 with a 116-win team. This right fielder collected over 4,300 combined professional hits in Japan and America and was elected to Cooperstown in 2025, one vote shy of unanimous. For 10 points, name this longtime Seattle Mariners star from Japan.
answer: Ichiro Suzuki [accept either name; accept Ichiro]

question: In a rant about this activity, one athlete repeated its name over twenty times and asked, "We're sitting here talking about" it, "not a game." That 2002 press conference by Allen Iverson made this word a punchline. A different athlete, Kawhi Leonard, popularized resting from games entirely under the term "load management," skipping this activity's in-game equivalent. For 10 points, (*) name this routine team activity that Iverson insisted was "not the game" he was paid to play.

This player hit 62 home runs in 2022 to break Roger Maris's American League single-season record. In the 2024 World Series, this player's dropped fly ball opened the door for a five-run Dodgers inning. Standing six-foot-seven, he was drafted out of Fresno State and won a Home Run Derby as a rookie in 2017. He was named captain of his team in 2023 after re-signing for (*) 360 million dollars, spurning the Giants. For 10 points, name this slugging outfielder for the New York Yankees.

At one Olympics, this athlete won a race by finishing ahead of silver medalist by over ten seconds—a margin so large that NBC's broadcast showed her alone in the pool. This swimmer won the 800-meter freestyle at four consecutive Olympics beginning in London 2012, when she was 15. Her dominance in distance events includes holding the world records in both the 800 and (*) 1500 freestyle. For 10 points, name this American widely considered the greatest female distance swimmer ever.

One of these events at the 1999 Women's World Cup ended with Brandi Chastain ripping off her jersey after converting against China. A men's World Cup final was first decided by one of these events in 1994, when Roberto Baggio skied his attempt over the bar. In the 2022 final, Emiliano Martínez's antics helped Argentina win one of these tiebreakers against France. Goalkeepers must keep one foot on the line during, (*) for 10 points, what method of deciding drawn knockout matches from twelve yards?
answer: penalty shootout [accept penalty kicks; prompt on "penalties"; prompt on "PKs"]

question: This team's home stadium sells out on a season-ticket waiting list estimated at several decades long, and its shares—which pay no dividends and cannot appreciate—have been sold to fans in occasional offerings, making it the NFL's only publicly owned franchise. Fans of this team celebrate touchdowns when players jump into the stands, a move called the (*) "Lambeau Leap." Its quarterbacks from 1992 to 2022 were essentially just Brett Favre and Aaron Rodgers. For 10 points, name this NFC North team whose fans wear foam cheese wedges.

This golfer completed the "Tiger Slam" by holding all four major titles simultaneously across 2000 and 2001. His 12-stroke victory at the 1997 Masters made him that tournament's youngest champion. After multiple back surgeries and a public scandal, he completed one of sport's great comebacks by winning the (*) 2019 Masters, his fifth green jacket. He shares the PGA Tour career wins record of 82 with Sam Snead. For 10 points, name this golfer with 15 major titles, second only to Jack Nicklaus.

This horse's owner won it in a coin flip that was actually considered a loss at the time. Ridden by Ron Turcotte, this horse set still-standing track records in all three legs of its most famous achievement, including a 1:59 and 2/5 Derby in which it ran each quarter-mile faster than the last. Its 31-length victory at the (*) Belmont Stakes prompted announcer Chic Anderson to say it was "moving like a tremendous machine." For 10 points, name this 1973 Triple Crown winner, often called the greatest racehorse ever.

As a rookie, this player famously crossed over Michael Jordan after leaving Georgetown, where he played for John Thompson. In the 2001 Finals, he stepped over Tyronn Lue after hitting a shot in his team's only win against the Lakers. Listed at six feet and 165 pounds, he won the 2001 MVP with the 76ers and wore his signature (*) arm sleeve and cornrows. For 10 points, name this Philadelphia guard nicknamed "The Answer," famous for a rant about practice.
answer: Allen Iverson [or Allen Ezail Iverson; accept "The Answer" before mention]

question: This athlete jogged and thumped his chest before the finish line of a 2008 Olympic final and still broke the world record. The following year in Berlin, he lowered the 100-meter mark to 9.58 seconds, which still stands. This sprinter completed the 100 and 200 double at three consecutive Olympics from Beijing to (*) Rio, striking his signature "lightning" pose after wins. For 10 points, name this Jamaican, the fastest man in recorded history.
answer: Usain Bolt [or Usain St. Leo Bolt]
